reason:
Refuted: the load-bearing claim in part (b) is factually wrong about the artifact, and part (a) is a misreading of the declared register whose fix would make the screen worse.

(b) is wrong. Measured at 1440x960 in both colour schemes, the publish screen emits NO h1.b-who. render-b.js states.publish (:1336) renders bar(F.project.name, ...), which puts the couple's name in .b-switch at 15px Geist / weight 600 / sentence case / -0.015em / 100% ink, and again as .b-pressTitle at 48px sans. The only 12px/0.20em/uppercase rendering of the couple's name on that screen is .b-ogWho INSIDE the unfurl card. So the asserted collision - 'the couple's name is emitted as an <h1> at the same 12px/0.20em/uppercase' alongside the captions, 'all three are one typographic object' - cannot occur: one of the three is not on the screen. The finding is describing a frame that does not exist.

The separation it asks for is already built. b.css:60-62 carries the comment 'The publish screen's own captions are the machine speaking' and drops .b-press .b-who to fore-62 while the owner-written identity line elsewhere (owner-empty, owner-flight, day, ended) stays at full --fore. Measured: h1.b-who = rgb(255,255,255); p.b-who on publish = rgba(255,255,255,0.62). That is exactly one ink step, the mechanism the round-6 comment names, already applied to precisely these two strings.

'Nothing at all separating' .b-ogWho from the captions is contradicted by the frame. In approach-publish--1440x960.png 'MARA & FINN' sits inside a white-plated, rounded, ink-filled simulacrum of a third-party chat card - two containers deep, ~120px below and ~50px right of 'WHAT LANDS IN THE MESSAGE', directly above a 96px numeral. The plate is a medium boundary, and the caption's entire job is to say the object below it is a different medium. That the card's ceremonial line matches the app's ceremonial line is correct, not a leak: it is the same object rendered elsewhere.

(a) misreads the register. The finding treats the prose word 'SECTION HEADS' in the b.css:1296 comment as a formal taxonomy, but the declared contract is shell.css:56, which names --track-label: 0.16em as 'uppercase mono micro-labels'. .b-inert honours that. On owner-empty the only other element at the identical spec is .b-label ('THE DAY') - a form field label, not a section head; there is no section head anywhere on that screen, so no reader is 'handed a section head where a control was'. .b-todayLabel ('Today is 16 July') is a marker and .b-behindLabel a disclosure label - the tier is micro-labels, and round 6 removed content strings (dates, counts, units, origin, where, keeper, wordmark) from it, not chrome labels. Note also that the wordmark named in the finding's own id is already fixed: .b-foot span renders 'Signal Timeline' sentence case at track-data, visible in the frame.

The ink clause it quotes is already satisfied. 'State and provenance sit one ink step behind' is about INK: .b-behindState, .b-keeper, .b-hiddenMark and .b-foot span are fore-62, and .b-inert is measured at rgba(255,255,255,0.62) - the same step. The only residue is case and tracking, and that is where the fix hurts.

The fix would make it worse. .b-inert lives inside .b-barActs among .b-act buttons (15px sans, sentence case, some ink-filled). The uppercase micro-label register is the only thing making 'SENDING COMES NEXT' read as chrome annotation rather than a second control beside the filled 'Copy the link' - which is the exact hazard render-b.js:470 writes down ('Anything not built is inert text, never a focusable promise'). Setting it to sentence-case mono at --track-data/fore-62 drops it into the provenance and .b-note voice inside an action row, where it reads as leftover machine prose adjacent to a primary button. Same at top-right on owner-empty.

The .b-pressCap half buys nothing measurable. Both captions and the h1 are already ink-separated; the proposal changes 12px to 11px and 0.20em to 0.16em on two strings that are structurally the top line of their column - which is what .b-who is for - and pays a new selector and two render-b.js edits for it. That is taste, not a defect at 9.5.

One thing the finding gets right and is credited: it does NOT repeat the prior round's error - it moves captions down the tracking ladder, away from the ceremonial step, not onto it. But being safe is not being needed.
